[7] Jenna: Charles. Jenna. Nice to meet you.
[8] Elizabeth: Elizabeth. Nice to meet you.
[9] Phil: Hey Jenna. I'm Phil.
[10] Jenna: Phil! My favorite radio voice!
[11] Phil: Oh. Thank you!
[12] Jillian: Jillian. Hi. Nice to meet you.
[13] Neal: Hey Jenna. I'm Neal.
[14] Phil: [in fake voice] Hi Jenna, I'm Phil.
[15] Neal: All right.
[16] Jenna: Okay. Thank you for having me. I'm Jenna Sereni. I am the founder and CEO of HandsDown, the first shopping platform built for communities and friends. So how many of you are in a group text with your friends? Or family? Yep, everybody. Okay. I'm on a group chat with my college friends. Well, a couple of years ago, we came together and decided to share our favorite things with each other that year. We made a spreadsheet, we each got a tab, and we tasked each other with just sharing our ten favorite things of the year. So we didn't really think much of the activity; we went about our days. But we quickly became obsessed with it, and we bought everything. My background is that I help pioneer influencer marketing. And my best friend has been in product at Etsy for over 12 years and she and I looked at each other and said, oh my gosh - we all just bought everything. As we had all of these people in this spreadsheet for a two-year period, we started tracking conversions and we found that our 24 friends over two and a-half years spent almost $34,000, which was about an annual average of $850 - 1000 per person. Well, a lightbulb went off. So HandsDown is a mobile app where you can share your absolute favorite things and favorite things by category. So your skincare routine, your favorite scary movies, the best finds at Trader Joes, the best vegan snacks. And we're also building tools for curators and creators and brands, so that you can share with communities that you relate to. We find that this is a $100 billion market opportunity across social commerce and retail media. Now 92% of consumers trust friends and family over all other sources of advertising or marketing. Word of mouth is by far the most powerful tool in building loyal relationships between consumers and brands and we're productizing that. Now at HandsDown, we are about to raise our seed round of $4 million to help us to scale our technology and our user growth, and help consumers to connect, discover, shop and earn together.
[17] Jillian: So how much have you raised on the 4 million?
[18] Jenna: So we have about a million dollars soft circled in the $4 million round. We are still talking to leads.
[19] Elizabeth: How many, how many users do you have?
[20] Jenna: Right now, we have about 4500 users. And I do have a demo for you as well, if you'd like.
[21] Jillian: Love to see the demo.
[22] Jenna: We've got a QR code.
Jenna walks the investors through the Hands Down app. Where you can see top 10 lists from your friends, your favorite influencers, or communities like the Brooklyn moms or crazy Eagles fans. It’s kind of like, if Pinterest and Wirecutter had a baby. Here’s Phil.
[23] Phil: What is the revenue model?
[24] Jenna: So allowing for brands to create a brand account and attach their back-end experience so that consumers can actually shop their brand in a universal shopping cart without ever leaving the HandsDown app. We earn anywhere from a 12 to 40% commission on those purchases. Where that gets really interesting is when you're in a micro-community like the Brooklyn moms, who, you know, love Bombas socks and it's back to school - Bombas can serve them a special offer in which we would earn a rev share on that.
[25] Elizabeth: So Jenna, I think, just to be very direct, there have been a number of folks who have tried this type of approach. I'm curious if you have any insights or learnings from either past failings or from talking with other entrepreneurs, or what you think is different here than what others have done.
[26] Jenna: One thing is the biggest challenge for us, it's the indexing of all of this data. It's how do we really present this data in an organized way within search and in a way that makes it truly valuable for people, and that's something that I think some other platforms have struggled with. The other thing is in acquisition. So essentially, if we just go out there with a media model, right, and we're trying to acquire users on Meta platforms and such, we're going to be competing with the brands that we want to be partnering with. So instead, we're going for a community-based acquisition model. We're actually going to be leveraging creators to bring audiences in and experts. We call them really curators. We incentivize them to bring their people in. So they earn when they bring in an acquisition and they earn when that person engages as well.
[27] Charles: And why do it on HandsDown as opposed to Linktr.ee or some other link in bio? If you already have an audience, like why do it on HandsDown as opposed to on -
[28] Jenna: So they have so many platforms to engage with. One of the things that the curators have shared with us is that a) the platforms don't always allow for them to use their affiliate links. We want them to still be able to earn when people shop their recommendations. The other thing is we just want to provide the technology that makes it so easy to host a top ten list. Right now, they have to post on Instagram stories, they have to create videos, they have to take photos, they have to, you know code a blog, they have to have a TikTok video, edit it - it's a lot of work. We want to create a really low-lift way for them to share top ten lists that they can earn commissions off of.
[29] Charles: Yeah. I just bring up the link in bio because if the link - especially for people who have decent audience, a lot of them, even within verticals there's a link in bio just designed for beauty, there's ones to - and there is, like, there is certainly like a lot of energy around this, particularly for the people who have audience already.
[30] Jenna: Yeah, definitely. We see this as like the perfect addition to a Linktr.ee. It's not for every single creator out there. We're not trying to provide a tool for MrBeast. We're not. And I literally - I actually was a part of creating the model that influencer marketing is today, so I always like to say first, I'm sorry. Second of all, we learned a lot, we're going to burn it to the ground and start fresh.
[31] Neal: So who are we up against? Who's doing this right right now that you're learning from?
[32] Jenna: So our biggest competition is LTK. LTK stands for Like To Know, they merged with RewardStyle, they recently got a $2 billion valuation. And what they do is they allow for influencers to make their content shoppable. Now, they're known for having really strict terms, and as far as who can be an LTK influencer, you kind of have to be the perfect woman. And we want to really create something for the people, something that shows that everyone matters, you don't have to be perfect and beautiful in the photo and make your life look absolutely perfect in order for your recommendations to matter. We see Wirecutter as being really amazing. And then of course Pinterest, who has been trying for years to make their content shoppable And, you know, I think what we want to create is something that's complimentary to Pinterest.
[33] Charles: On a related note, I'm curious, like the, the original sort of group chat thing you explained, I was like, oh that feels like a product space where there isn't a good solution today, and this one feels like it's just a much more crowded environment. I'm curious, like the - is the hypothesis that by being, just having used the app, by being on the app, I'm going to get inspired by things that other people who are not in my friends circle have discovered or put on the app and that this browse and discover is going to expand? Because the first product you mentioned to me felt much more contained.
[34] Jillian: Yeah.
[35] Phil: I have to say, Charles, I had the exact same feeling. When she first described the experience of interacting with her friends and sharing their favorite things, that really sounded interesting to me and something like I might even do. And then when you talked about the model as you envision it, I thought, wow, there's a lot of competition in that space.
[36] Jenna: Yeah, so you'll still be able to do all of that. They could be micro or they could be macro communities. So macro being like the Brooklyn moms, which has 45,000 Facebook followers and all the recommendations kind of get lost in the ether, But then there's the group chat. That's a micro-community that you could actually host privately. And so that's something that we're creating, is somewhere that you can actually create a circle with your friends, this community, where you can share favorite things privately, just as your small circle of people.
[37] Elizabeth: I feel like, and being very direct here, I think it's hard to actually be both of those. I think you are either one or the other. So if you're in the small group, it's all about small groups and then you have to somehow figure out how to take somebody in a small group and have them invite other people into a whole new group. Or you're more in the Pinterest category of, you know, let's get everybody and their mother to see my boards and now I'm trying to show everybody my taste. But I feel like trying to message both is going to be very challenging. And actually that - I think that product in this space matters so much and all these little nuances matter so much and I'm not sure I quite see you in one category or the other, so for that reason I'm out. Thank you.
[38] Jenna: Thank you.
[39] Neal: I'm curious to know, is there some form of a long form assessment like the Wirecutter? There's a lot of trust there. So if I need to buy something, I go there and that's my friend. Right. The Wirecutter is my - even better than my friends when it comes to choosing certain things.
[40] Jenna: Some of the things that we've considered, are, you know, giving creators more of a space to kind of create their environment within the application. You know, almost create their page that houses their whole pop-up shop of recommendations, right. That can kind of help to solve for that.
[41] Neal: Got it.
[42] Jenna: yeah.
[43] Jillian: Does that answer your question?
[44] Neal: Somewhat. I mean, one example would be short form video content as a form of reviewing the products, right? And getting more people to engage there.
[45] Jenna: Definitely.
[46] Neal: Okay.
[47] Jenna: That's a big part of our plan with this native app. We've kind of, you know, we wanted to start slow. We've been sort of bootstrapping. You know, we have a really impressive team considering what we've raised and what we've done in a short period of time. But especially myself as - my expertise is in commerce driving content, so that is like, you know, exactly where I want to go, I just want to do it really smartly. I don't want to throw out all of the product experiences that the other platforms have kind of, for the sake of competing with each other, and really think about what the right content opportunity is for this specific experience.
[48] Neal: Got it. Thank you.
[49] Charles: I think like Elizabeth, I think I'm out too. But for maybe like a slightly - related but different reason. I think this sort of shop with your friends social - this is in that category of things that should work. It should be something that works, and it - it sort of hasn't yet. And I think it - there's some behavioral insight that's missing around like why none of the products that have been built connect the dots on that behavior, and it's sort of in that, like, people should do this! And I think 'should' is a very dangerous word when you're building a product. And I keep coming back to the fact that the product I'm really excited about was the first one you described. And if the company was like laser focused on that, I would be able to go way down the rabbit hole with you. And that's an experiment I think that hasn't been run, and where we don't have as much data. But a good way to lose money as an investor is to fall in love with something that the founder is not as focused on as you are. So for me, personally, I'm out. But if at any point you decide to go deeper on the sort of small group social sharing, I just think about how many links and pointers to products get shared in my group chat, I would love to have that conversation in the future, but only if that's something you decide you want to make the focus of the company.
[50] Jenna: It's great feedback. Thank you. We found that Google Sheets fulfilled that for us.
[51] Charles: Alright good answer.
[52] Jenna: But thank you. That's very, very valuable.
[53] Phil: For similar - very similar reasons, this isn't a fit for me, either. I was excited by the genesis of the company, and then I started envisioning how you might productize that. But then you veered in a different direction and one that I see as crowded and I don't see enough likelihood of success. and I want to see where that - where that lands as a product before, you know, taking a hard look at it.

taxonomy.label: business_model_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's perception of the startup’s revenue model, monetization approach, or service/automation mix as a driver of business viability.

taxonomy.label: business_viability_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's concern that the overall business viability, model, or economics are not sufficiently compelling.

taxonomy.label: capital_intensity_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that the startup will require substantial ongoing capital investment, increasing risk or misalignment with the investor’s funding capacity.

taxonomy.label: competitive_advantage_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s beliefs about what drives defensibility or sustainable competitive advantage in a market.

taxonomy.label: competitive_intensity_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that the category is highly competitive, attention‐constrained, and requires heavy marketing to win, reducing the likelihood of outsized success.

taxonomy.label: competitive_landscape_inertia
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the difficulty of displacing or changing behavior of incumbents due to entrenched solutions, habits, or workflows.

taxonomy.label: deal_terms_complexity_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s concern that the structure or details of deal terms (e.g., convertibles, SAFEs, preferred terms) may introduce complexity, ambiguity, or unfavorable outcomes.

taxonomy.label: decision_context_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to constraints imposed by the specific evaluation format, environment, or context rather than the startup's fundamentals.

taxonomy.label: dilution_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s concern that the financing plan will cause excessive dilution relative to their ownership goals or stage fit.

taxonomy.label: execution_risk_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s concern that the team may not yet have demonstrated sufficient execution reliability or maturity for the risk level of the round.

taxonomy.label: founder_equity_incentive_alignment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to ensuring founders retain sufficient ownership to remain properly motivated, aligned, and incentivized for the long-term company‐building journey.

taxonomy.label: founder_execution
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception of the founders' execution ability, resourcefulness, pace, and operational grit.

taxonomy.label: founder_market_fit
taxonomy.definition: Rationales based on how well the founder's background, experience, or motivation aligns with the target market.

taxonomy.label: founder_qualities
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's perception of the founders' personal traits, capabilities, or appeal.

taxonomy.label: founder_skillset
taxonomy.definition: Rationales tied to the founder's core skills or functional strengths relevant to company-building.

taxonomy.label: fund_economics_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales tied to the investor’s fund size, check size, or ownership goals that constrain how selective they must be when choosing investments.

taxonomy.label: fundraising_demand_signal
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception that the company will attract capital easily due to current or expected investor demand.

taxonomy.label: growth_projection_risk
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that the company’s growth, revenue, or user‐scale projections are insufficiently modeled, unrealistic, or lack credible underlying assumptions.

taxonomy.label: investment_thesis_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's predefined investment thesis or mandate that restricts them to specific sectors, business models, or company types.

taxonomy.label: investment_upside_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's view that the risk‐reward profile offers disproportionately large potential returns relative to downside risk.

taxonomy.label: investor_domain_knowledge_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor lacking the necessary domain knowledge to effectively assess the technology, moat, competition, or overall viability of the opportunity.

taxonomy.label: investor_experience_bias
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's prior personal experiences, wins, losses, or operational history that shape their judgment of a new opportunity.

taxonomy.label: market_entry_path_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception that there is a clear, reachable initial customer segment that can serve as an effective wedge into the larger market.

taxonomy.label: market_problem_validation
taxonomy.definition: Rationales tied to the investor perceiving the underlying problem as real, important, or painful enough to support a venture-scale solution.

taxonomy.label: market_size_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s belief about the absolute or relative size and fluidity of the addressable market.

taxonomy.label: market_timing
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's belief that the timing is favorable or unfavorable for this market, category, or product to emerge or scale.

taxonomy.label: mission_alignment_preference
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's personal or emotional alignment with the startup's mission or purpose.

taxonomy.label: portfolio_conflict_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to constraints arising from existing portfolio investments that create competitive conflicts preventing a new investment.

taxonomy.label: product_adoption
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to evidence that end users are adopting and using the product meaningfully.

taxonomy.label: product_appeal_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s positive perception of the product’s appeal, quality, or desirability based on their own reaction.

taxonomy.label: product_differentiation_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to how unique, defensible, or hard-to-copy the product or technology is perceived to be.

taxonomy.label: product_success_factor_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to which product components or attributes are perceived as most essential to the startup's ability to succeed.

taxonomy.label: solution_feasibility_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's belief that the proposed product or solution is technically or operationally feasible.

taxonomy.label: stage_valuation_mismatch
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception of a mismatch between the company’s stage of progress and the valuation being requested.

taxonomy.label: traction_repeatability_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that current traction, usage, or revenue signals are too early or insufficiently repeatable to support scaling.

taxonomy.label: unit_economics_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception that the business benefits from structurally attractive unit economics, such as profitable or self-reinforcing customer acquisition.

taxonomy.label: venture_scale_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that the companys market dynamics, ceiling, or competitive landscape limit its ability to achieve venture-scale outcomes.

taxonomy.label: investor_value_add_fit
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about whether the investor can contribute meaningful help, networks, or domain value beyond capital to this specific company.

taxonomy.label: founder_coachability_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about how receptive the founder is to feedback, advice, or course-correction and their ability to read and respond to the room.

taxonomy.label: founder_communication_quality
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about the founder's clarity, articulation, command of their numbers, and storytelling ability when presenting the business.

taxonomy.label: founder_motivation_authenticity
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about the genuineness, personal connection, or origin of the founder's drive to work on this particular problem.

taxonomy.label: go_to_market_strategy_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about how the company will reach and acquire customers, including sales motion, channel scalability, and cost of acquisition.

taxonomy.label: founder_investor_vision_alignment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about whether the founder's intended direction or focus for the company aligns with the path the investor believes in or would back.

taxonomy.label: corporate_structure_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales tied to the company's legal entity, incorporation, jurisdiction, or IP-ownership structure as a barrier or condition to investing.
